newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Hashimoto policy speech eagerly awaited in SE Asia.
newsitem.headline: Hashimoto policy speech eagerly awaited in SE Asia.

text.p: Southeast Asia is awaiting eagerly a major policy speech by Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto in Singapore that winds up his five-nation tour of the region, Singapore analysts said on Friday.

"I think we are all keen to hear what exactly this 'Hashimoto principle' is," one analyst of regional politics said regarding the speech the Japanese leader is due to deliver on Tuesday before flying back home.

Hashimoto, at the end of visits to Brunei, Malaysia, Indonesia, Vietnam and Singapore, is scheduled to lay out Japan's policy on the Asia-Pacific region and enunciate what aides call "the Hashimoto principle".
"From the Southeast Asian point of view, we are looking to Japan to provide leadership in economic and political terms," said the analyst, who declined to be identified.
"Japan is the most potent player in the region and therefore any enhancement of its involvement would be welcome," he said.

He and other analysts, who also declined to be identified, said economically booming Asia was entering a tricky phase, with Chinese influence growing while there were lingering doubts about long-term U.S. commitment to stability.

"The general view is that China is no longer interested in territorial expansion and there should be no great worries on that score. China is too preoccupied with its economic development to meddle abroad," another analyst told Reuters.
"But they will probably develop their military might as a way of protecting their economic interests and, if someone rattles them, there would be a response," he said.
"That's where Japan comes in. It is in the interests both of Japan and Southeast Asia to engage China in a multilateral security arrangement and to use economic linkages to build relations," he said.
"Especially in economic terms, Japan is seen as the balancer as the United States turns its attention to other parts of the world," said another analyst.

During his tour, Hashimoto was meeting some of the most influential figures in the seven-nation Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), which groups Brunei, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam.
In Kuala Lumpur he had discussions with Malaysian Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad and was scheduled to hold substantive talks with Indonesian President Suharto on Friday.
In Singapore, where he is scheduled to arrive on Sunday, he is to hold talks with Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong before giving his policy speech.
The analysts said the talks would probably centre on strategic Asian issues, with the focus on economic development as the prime source of regional stability.
"The first line of policy on China is economic engagement and here Singapore and Japan seem to think much along the same lines," said the third analyst.
"Neither has the domestic resources or labour pool to compete globally from a home base and they have to invest abroad," he said. "Both are investing in China."
He said Goh was also likely to urge Hashimoto to encourage continued growth of Japanese investment in the ASEAN region, which accounts for 16 percent of Japan's trade.
"Southeast Asia has great potential for further development and is in desperate need of more foreign investment. Japan's involvement is extremely important".
